citation.title: Average treatment effects in the presence of unknown interference

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 3.1, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] Consider a sample of $n$ units indexed by the set $\mathbf{U} = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. An experimenter intervenes on the world in ways that potentially affect the units. The intervention is described by a $n$-dimensional binary vector $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n) \in \{0, 1\}^n$. For short, we refer to $z_i$ as unit $i$'s treatment. Each unit has a function $y_i : \{0, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ denoting the observed outcome for the unit under a specific and potentially counterfactual intervention. In particular, $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ is the response of $i$ when the intervention is $\mathbf{z}$. We refer to the elements of the image of this function as potential outcomes. Let $\mathbf{z}_{-i} = (z_1, \ldots, z_{i-1}, z_{i+1}, \ldots, z_n)$ denote the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\mathbf{z}$. The potential outcome $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ can then be written as $y_i(z_i; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. Throughout the paper, we assume that the potential outcomes are well-defined. The experimenter sets $\mathbf{z}$ according to a random vector $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)$. The probability distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ is the design of the experiment. The design is the sole source of randomness we will consider. Let $Y_i$ denote the observed outcome of unit $i$: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z})$. As above, $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ denotes $\mathbf{Z}$ without its $i$th element, so $Y_i = y_i(Z_i; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})$. [No interference: Section 3.2, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] It is conventional to assume that the potential outcomes are restricted so a unit's outcome is only affected by its own treatment. That is, for any two assignments $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}'$, if the treatment of a given unit is the same for both assignments, then the outcome for that unit is also the same. This no-interference assumption admits a definition of the treatment effect $\tau_i$ for unit $i$: $\tau_i = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$, where $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$ is any element of $\{0, 1\}^{n-1}$. [Definitions 1 to 3: p. 677 (PDF p. 5)] DEFINITION 1. Under no interference, the average treatment effect (ATE) is the average unit-level treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i$. The assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effect is $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i}) = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 2. An assignment-conditional average treatment effect is the average of the assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effects under a given assignment: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 3. The expected average treatment effect (EATE) is the expected assignment-conditional average treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$, where the expectation is taken over the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ given by the experimental design. [Definition 4: p. 678 (PDF p. 6)] DEFINITION 4. The average distributional shift effect (ADSE) is the average difference between the conditional expected outcomes for the two treatment conditions: $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]\right)$. [Interference indicator: Section 4, p. 680 (PDF p. 8)] We say that unit $i$ interferes with unit $j$ if changing $i$'s treatment changes $j$'s outcome under at least one treatment assignment. We also say that a unit interferes with itself even if its own treatment does not affect its outcome. The indicator $I_{ij}$ denotes such interference: $I_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } y_j(\mathbf{z}) \ne y_j(\mathbf{z}') \text{ for some } \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \{0, 1\}^n \text{ such that } \mathbf{z}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}'_{-i}, \\ 1 & \text{if } i = j, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Definition 5 (Interference dependence): p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ where $d_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } I_{\ell i} I_{\ell j} = 1 \text{ for some } \ell \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ The sum $d_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ gives the number of interference dependencies for unit $i$. [Interference counts: p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $c_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} I_{ij}$ and $C_p = \left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^p\right]^{1/p}$. We write $C_\infty$ for the limit of $C_p$ as $p \to \infty$, which is the maximum $c_i$ over $\mathbf{U}$. [Asymptotic regime: Section 5, pp. 681–682 (PDF pp. 9–10)] We consider an arbitrary sequence of samples indexed by their sample size. The samples are not assumed to be drawn from some larger population or otherwise randomly generated. All quantities describing the samples, such as the potential outcomes and experimental designs, have their own sequences also indexed by $n$. But we leave the indexing implicit as no confusion arises. [Definition 6: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] The Horvitz–Thompson (HT) and Hájek (HÁ) estimators are $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i}$ and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i}{p_i}\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1 - Z_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$, where $p_i = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$ is the marginal treatment probability for unit $i$. [Assumption 1: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] We assume throughout the remainder of the paper that the experimental design and potential outcomes are sufficiently well behaved, as formalized in the following assumption. ASSUMPTION 1 (Regularity conditions). There exist constants $k < \infty$, $q \ge 2$ and $s \ge 1$ such that for all $i \in \mathbf{U}$ in the sequence of samples: A (Probabilistic assignment). $k^{-1} \le \Pr(Z_i = 1) \le 1 - k^{-1}$, B (Outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|Y_i|^q] \le k^q$, C (Potential outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})|^s] \le k^s$ for $z \in \{0, 1\}$. [Assumption 2: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] ASSUMPTION 2 (Restricted interference). $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = o(n)$. [Bernoulli design: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] We call this a Bernoulli randomization design, and it satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i^{z_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - z_i}$ for some set of assignment probabilities $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ bounded away from zero and one. [Complete randomization: p. 684 (PDF p. 12)] $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} \binom{n}{m}^{-1} & \text{if } \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i = m, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}$ where $m = \lfloor pn \rfloor$ for some fixed $p$ strictly between zero and one. We call the design complete randomization. [Paired randomization: p. 685 (PDF p. 13)] It is implicit that the sample size is even so that all units are paired. Let $\rho : \mathbf{U} \to \mathbf{U}$ describe a pairing so that $\rho(i) = j$ indicates that units $i$ and $j$ are paired. The pairing is symmetric, so the self-composition of $\rho$ is the identity function. The paired randomization design then satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} 2^{-n/2} & \text{if } z_i \ne z_{\rho(i)} \text{ for all } i \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Notation the paper uses without defining] The paper does not define $\mathcal{O}_p$, $o_p$, 'consistent' or 'root-$n$ consistent'. The proof of Lemma A5 (Supplement A, p. 4) uses $X_n - x_n = \mathcal{O}_p(a_n)$ in the sense that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are a constant $\kappa$ and an $N$ such that $\Pr(|X_n - x_n| \ge \kappa a_n) \le \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$. 'Consistent for' an estimand means that the difference between the estimator and the estimand (both sequences in $n$) converges in probability to zero; 'root-$n$ consistent' means that this difference is $\mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5})$. Supplement A is the separate file 'Supplement A: Proofs' (41 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPA) and Supplement B is 'Supplement B: Simulation study' (21 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPB); their page numbers are their own printed page numbers, which equal their PDF page numbers. In the main article the printed page number is the PDF page number plus 672.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Proposition 1, first paragraph and last sentences: the choice of the subsequence, corrected
canonical_claim.location: Supplement A, Section 4, proof of Proposition 1: first paragraph, p. 6, and the last sentences of the proof, p. 7
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected step] Let $L = \limsup_{n \to \infty} n^{-1}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$. Failure of Assumption 2 gives $L > 0$. Choose $0 < c < L$. The definition of the limit superior implies that $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} \ge cn$ happens infinitely often. On this subsequence, use the displayed potential outcomes with $\lambda = L$. In the final paragraph, refer to this selected subsequence rather than asserting that the original sequence meets $Ln$ infinitely often. [Formal content] (i) For a real sequence $(a_n)$ with $L = \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n > 0$ and any $c$ with $0 < c < L$, the set $\{n : a_n \ge c\}$ is infinite. (The set $\{n : a_n \ge L\}$ can be finite: the counterexample target for this finding.) (ii) The rest of the proof is unchanged. For each $n$ in the selected subsequence, with $M_n = \lceil L^{0.5}n\rceil$ and the displayed potential outcomes with $\lambda = L$: $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \frac{M_n^2}{n} + \frac{n - M_n}{n} \ge Ln$ for the constructed outcomes, $|y_i(\mathbf{z})| \le L^{-0.5}$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \Pr(Z_1 = 1)$ and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = Z_1$, so that $|\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}| = |Z_1 - \Pr(Z_1 = 1)| \ge k^{-1}$ with probability one for every $n$ in the subsequence. For $n$ outside the subsequence the potential outcomes may be set to zero. Hence the HT estimator does not converge in probability to EATE, which is Proposition 1 for the HT estimator; the Hájek estimator is treated in the headline target for Proposition 1.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (i) is a statement about real sequences and involves no probability. The identities in (ii) are exact for each fixed $n$ and any design satisfying Assumption 1A; they are listed with locations in the target for Proposition 1.
canonical_claim.note: Corrected text as settled in validated.json (the corrected text recorded with the prior correction; Sol's smallest repair keeps $\lambda = \limsup$ in the construction and uses a separate constant $c$ only to select the subsequence, so that the limit superior of the constructed sequence is still $L$). No assumption is added and Proposition 1 is unchanged.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6.3, the sentence on Theorem 2.7 of Chen and Shao (2004): a normal approximation for the HT estimator under the Bernoulli design if $d_{\mathrm{MAX}} = \mathcal{O}(1)$, as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 693 (PDF p. 21), Section 6.3 (Tail bounds), first paragraph
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [p. 693 (PDF p. 21), Section 6.3] Such approximations may be reasonable when the interference is very sparse. For example, Theorem 2.7 in Chen and Shao (2004) can be applied to the HT point estimator under the Bernoulli design if $d_{\mathrm{MAX}} = \mathcal{O}(1)$, showing that the sampling distribution is approximately normal in large samples. This condition is, however, stronger than Assumption 2. [What is refuted] That a Bernoulli design, Assumption 1 and $d_{\mathrm{MAX}} = \mathcal{O}(1)$ suffice for the sampling distribution of $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, centered at $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ and scaled by its standard deviation, to be approximately normal in large samples. [Counterexample, from the validator] For each $n \ge 1$ let $Z_1, \ldots, Z_n$ be independent Bernoulli($\frac{1}{2}$), $y_1(\mathbf{z}) = z_1$ and $y_i(\mathbf{z}) = 0$ for $i \ge 2$. Then Assumption 1 holds with $k = 2$ and every $q \ge 2$, $s \ge 1$; $I_{ij} = d_{ij} = \mathbb{1}[i = j]$, so $d_{\mathrm{MAX}} = d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = 1$; $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = 1/n$; $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = 2Z_1/n$; $\mathrm{E}[\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}] = 1/n$; $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = 1/n^2$; and $R_n = (\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}})/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})} = 2Z_1 - 1$, so $\Pr(R_n = -1) = \Pr(R_n = 1) = \frac{1}{2}$ for every $n$. For every continuous distribution function $G$, $\sup_x |\Pr(R_n \le x) - G(x)| \ge \frac{1}{4}$; in particular $R_n$ does not converge in distribution to the standard normal law. Also $n\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = 1/n \to 0$. [Second family, with an estimand that does not shrink] Same design, $y_1(\mathbf{z}) = z_1$ and $y_i(\mathbf{z}) = z_i - \frac{1}{2}$ for $i \ge 2$. Then all potential outcomes have absolute value at most 1, $d_{\mathrm{MAX}} = 1$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = 1$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = (n - 1 + 2Z_1)/n$, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = 1/n^2$ and again $R_n = 2Z_1 - 1$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'. [$d_{\mathrm{MAX}}$: p. 692 (PDF p. 20)] $d_{\mathrm{MAX}}$ is the maximum of $d_i$ over $i \in \mathbf{U}$. [Reading of 'approximately normal in large samples', from the validator] With $V_n = \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})$, the standardized estimator $R_n = (\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}})/\sqrt{V_n}$ converges in distribution to the standard normal law. The Kolmogorov distance between distribution functions $F$ and $G$ is $\sup_x |F(x) - G(x)|$.
canonical_claim.note: Rated an error, Minor. Every displayed fact is exact for each fixed $n$; the bound $\frac{1}{4}$ holds because the distribution function of $R_n$ jumps by $\frac{1}{2}$ at $-1$. No error in the theorem of Chen and Shao is alleged; the counterexample concerns the sufficiency of the condition stated in the paper. The first family is the one used for P009-E002.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6.3, the sentence on the normal approximation for the HT estimator under the Bernoulli design when $d_{\mathrm{MAX}} = \mathcal{O}(1)$, corrected
canonical_claim.location: p. 693 (PDF p. 21), Section 6.3 (Tail bounds), first paragraph
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected sentence] For example, under Assumption 1, a Bernoulli design and $d_{\mathrm{MAX}} = \mathcal{O}(1)$, the HT point estimator centered at EATE and divided by its true standard deviation is asymptotically standard normal provided $\liminf_{n \to \infty} n\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) > 0$. [In full] Consider a sequence of samples, each with a Bernoulli randomization design, such that Assumption 1 holds (constants $k < \infty$, $q \ge 2$, $s \ge 1$ not depending on $n$), $\sup_n d_{\mathrm{MAX}} < \infty$, and $\liminf_{n \to \infty} n\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) > 0$. Then $\frac{\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})}} \overset{d}{\longrightarrow} N(0, 1)$. Without the condition on the variance the conclusion can fail (the counterexample target for this finding). No statement is made about division by an estimated standard error.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'. [$d_{\mathrm{MAX}}$: p. 692 (PDF p. 20)] $d_{\mathrm{MAX}}$ is the maximum of $d_i$ over $i \in \mathbf{U}$. [Reading of 'approximately normal in large samples', from the validator] With $V_n = \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})$, the standardized estimator $R_n = (\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}})/\sqrt{V_n}$ converges in distribution to the standard normal law. The Kolmogorov distance between distribution functions $F$ and $G$ is $\sup_x |F(x) - G(x)|$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: For each fixed $n$, under a Bernoulli design: (a) $\mathrm{E}[\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}] = \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (Lemmas A1 and A8, Supplement A, pp. 3 and 7). (b) With $T_i = \frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} - \frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i T_i$, and $T_i$ is a function of the treatments $Z_\ell$ with $I_{\ell i} = 1$; if no $d_{ij}$ equals 1 between two sets of units, the two families of $T_i$ are independent (the graph with edges $d_{ij} = 1$ is a dependency graph), and each unit has at most $d_{\mathrm{MAX}}$ neighbours including itself. (c) The number of $\ell$ with $I_{\ell i} = 1$ is at most $d_i \le d_{\mathrm{MAX}}$, each configuration of those treatments has probability at least $k^{-d_{\mathrm{MAX}}}$, and $\mathrm{E}[|Y_i|^2] \le k^2$, so $|y_i(\mathbf{z})| \le k^{1 + d_{\mathrm{MAX}}/2}$ for every $\mathbf{z}$: the potential outcomes are uniformly bounded, which is why the exponent $q \ge 2$ of Assumption 1 suffices. (d) $\mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_i T_i\right) = n^2\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})$, which is at least $cn$ eventually for some $c > 0$ under the variance condition.
canonical_claim.note: Corrected sentence as settled in validated.json after the re-run of the validation: the original Assumption 1 with $q \ge 2$ is kept and only the variance lower bound is added. The validator's derivation proves the version with $q > 2$ by truncation and a cumulant bound for sums with a bounded-degree dependency graph; the re-run observes that bounded $d_{\mathrm{MAX}}$ already makes the potential outcomes uniformly bounded (finite lemma (c)), so $q > 2$ is not an extra requirement. The variance condition is sufficient, not necessary. The limit theorem itself (a central limit theorem under a bounded-degree dependency graph, which the paper attributes to Chen and Shao (2004), Theorem 2.7) is not in the staged sources; a formalizer may need to take it as a named assumption.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The paragraph before Proposition 5: under complete randomization with bounded interference, '$\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j)$ approaches zero for all pairs of units with $d_{ij} = 0$', as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 688 (PDF p. 16), first paragraph (before Proposition 5), third sentence
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [p. 688 (PDF p. 16)] Design mixing and design separation stipulate that the dependence between treatments are sufficiently rare or sufficiently weak (or some combination thereof). The assumptions encapsulate and extend the conditions in the previous sections. In particular, complete randomization under bounded interference constitutes a setting where dependence is weak: $\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j)$ approaches zero for all pairs of units with $d_{ij} = 0$. [What is refuted] Convergence to zero of the pair mixing coefficient for every pair with $d_{ij} = 0$ under complete randomization and $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \mathcal{O}(1)$. [Counterexample, from the validator] For each integer $r \ge 1$ let $n = 4r + 2$, $h = 2r + 1 = n/2$, $A = \{1\} \cup \{3, 4, \ldots, h + 1\}$ and $B = \{2\} \cup \{h + 2, h + 3, \ldots, 2h\}$ (disjoint, $h$ units each, $h$ odd). Let $\mathbf{Z}$ be uniform on the $\binom{n}{h}$ vectors with $\sum_\ell Z_\ell = h$ (complete randomization with $m = h$, $p = \frac{1}{2}$), and for every $\mathbf{z} \in \{0, 1\}^n$ let $y_1(\mathbf{z}) = h^{-1}\sum_{\ell \in A} z_\ell$, $y_2(\mathbf{z}) = h^{-1}\sum_{\ell \in B} z_\ell$ and $y_j(\mathbf{z}) = z_j$ for $3 \le j \le n$. Then: (a) all potential outcomes lie in $[0, 1]$ and $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = \frac{1}{2}$, so Assumption 1 holds with $k = 2$; (b) $I_{\ell 1} = 1$ if and only if $\ell \in A$, $I_{\ell 2} = 1$ if and only if $\ell \in B$, and for $j \ge 3$, $I_{\ell j} = 1$ if and only if $\ell = j$; hence $d_{12} = 0$; (c) $\sum_{i,j} d_{ij} = 3n - 4$, so $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = 3 - 4/n < 3$; $c_1 = c_2 = 1$ and $c_\ell = 2$ for $\ell \ge 3$, so $C_1 = 2 - 2/n$ and $C_\infty = 2$; (d) with $T_A = \sum_{\ell \in A} Z_\ell$ and $T_B = \sum_{\ell \in B} Z_\ell = h - T_A$, the events $E = \{T_A \ge (h + 1)/2\} \in \sigma(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_1)$ and $F = \{T_B \le (h - 1)/2\} \in \sigma(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_2)$ coincide and $\Pr(E) = \frac{1}{2}$, so $|\Pr(E \cap F) - \Pr(E)\Pr(F)| = \frac{1}{4}$ and $\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_1, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_2) = \frac{1}{4}$ for every $r \ge 1$. So the fixed pair of units 1 and 2 has $d_{12} = 0$ and a mixing coefficient equal to $\frac{1}{4}$ along the whole sequence $n = 4r + 2$, while $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} < 3$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'. [Assignment vectors affecting a unit: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i = (I_{1i}Z_1, I_{2i}Z_2, \ldots, I_{ni}Z_n)$. The vector is defined so that its $j$th element is $Z_j$ if unit $j$ is interfering with $i$, and zero otherwise. Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i}$ be the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i$. The definitions have the following convenient properties: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z}) = y_i(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i)$ and $y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) = y_i(z; \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})$. [Alpha-mixing coefficient: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For two random variables $X$ and $Y$ defined on the same probability space, let $\alpha(X, Y) = \sup_{x \in \sigma(X),\, y \in \sigma(Y)} \left|\Pr(x \cap y) - \Pr(x)\Pr(y)\right|$, where $\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(Y)$ denote the sub-sigma-algebras generated by the random variables. The coefficient $\alpha(X, Y)$ is zero if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent. The maximum is $\alpha(X, Y) = 1/4$. [Definition 9 (External and internal average mixing coefficients): p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For the maximum values of $q$ and $s$ such that Assumptions 1B and 1C hold, let $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(1 - d_{ij})\left[\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j)\right]^{\frac{q-2}{q}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\alpha(Z_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})\right]^{\frac{s-1}{s}}$, where $0^0$ is defined as zero to accommodate the cases $q = 2$ and $s = 1$. [Assumptions 5 and 6: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] ASSUMPTION 5 (Design mixing). $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = o(n)$. ASSUMPTION 6 (Design separation). $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = o(n)$. [Bounded interference: Corollary 1, p. 685 (PDF p. 13)] bounded interference, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \mathcal{O}(1)$.
canonical_claim.note: Rated an error, Minor. The facts (a) to (d) are exact for each $r$; that $\alpha \le \frac{1}{4}$ always is stated on p. 687. The sequence also satisfies Assumption 2 and $C_1 = o(n^{0.5})$, and the estimators are consistent in it, so no proposition is contradicted. The paper's later sentence in the same paragraph, on complete randomization under the conditions of Proposition 3, allows such rare pairs.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The paragraph before Proposition 5: the pair mixing coefficients under complete randomization with bounded interference, corrected
canonical_claim.location: p. 688 (PDF p. 16), first paragraph (before Proposition 5), third sentence
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected sentence] Under complete randomization with bounded average interference, $\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j)$ approaches zero uniformly for all but an asymptotically vanishing fraction of pairs with $d_{ij} = 0$; exceptional pairs can retain nonvanishing dependence. [In full] Consider a sequence of samples with complete randomization ($m$ treated units out of $n$, $0 < m < n$) and $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} \le D$ for all sufficiently large $n$, for a constant $D$. Let $N_0 = \{(i, j) : d_{ij} = 0\}$. Then there are sets $E_n \subseteq N_0$ such that $|E_n|/|N_0| \to 0$ and $\max_{(i,j) \in N_0 \setminus E_n}\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j) \to 0$. The set $E_n$ cannot in general be taken empty (the counterexample target for this finding).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'. [Assignment vectors affecting a unit: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i = (I_{1i}Z_1, I_{2i}Z_2, \ldots, I_{ni}Z_n)$. The vector is defined so that its $j$th element is $Z_j$ if unit $j$ is interfering with $i$, and zero otherwise. Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i}$ be the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i$. The definitions have the following convenient properties: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z}) = y_i(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i)$ and $y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) = y_i(z; \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})$. [Alpha-mixing coefficient: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For two random variables $X$ and $Y$ defined on the same probability space, let $\alpha(X, Y) = \sup_{x \in \sigma(X),\, y \in \sigma(Y)} \left|\Pr(x \cap y) - \Pr(x)\Pr(y)\right|$, where $\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(Y)$ denote the sub-sigma-algebras generated by the random variables. The coefficient $\alpha(X, Y)$ is zero if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent. The maximum is $\alpha(X, Y) = 1/4$. [Definition 9 (External and internal average mixing coefficients): p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For the maximum values of $q$ and $s$ such that Assumptions 1B and 1C hold, let $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(1 - d_{ij})\left[\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j)\right]^{\frac{q-2}{q}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\alpha(Z_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})\right]^{\frac{s-1}{s}}$, where $0^0$ is defined as zero to accommodate the cases $q = 2$ and $s = 1$. [Assumptions 5 and 6: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] ASSUMPTION 5 (Design mixing). $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = o(n)$. ASSUMPTION 6 (Design separation). $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = o(n)$. [Bounded interference: Corollary 1, p. 685 (PDF p. 13)] bounded interference, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \mathcal{O}(1)$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: From the validator's derivation (section 6), for each fixed $n$: write $a_i = \sum_{\ell} I_{\ell i}$ for the number of units interfering with $i$ and $t_n = \lfloor n^{1/4} \rfloor$. (a) $\sum_i a_i = \sum_\ell c_\ell = nC_1 \le n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$. (b) $|\{i : a_i > t_n\}| \le n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}/t_n$, so at most $2n^2 d_{\mathrm{AVG}}/t_n$ ordered pairs contain such a unit; $E_n$ is the set of those pairs that lie in $N_0$. (c) $|N_0| = n^2 - n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$. (d) If $d_{ij} = 0$, the sets $\{\ell : I_{\ell i} = 1\}$ and $\{\ell : I_{\ell j} = 1\}$ are disjoint; with $K = a_i + a_j \le n$, $\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j) \le 3\varepsilon_K$ where $\varepsilon_K = \frac{K(K - 1)}{2(n - K + 1)}$ bounds the total variation distance between the law of $K$ coordinates of $\mathbf{Z}$ under complete randomization and the law of $K$ independent Bernoulli($m/n$) variables. For pairs outside $E_n$, $K \le 2t_n$ and the bound is $\frac{3(2t_n)(2t_n - 1)}{2(n - 2t_n + 1)}$, which is of order $n^{-0.5}$.
canonical_claim.note: Corrected sentence as in Sol's smallest repair; the precise form with explicit exceptional sets and constants is the validator's. Only this explanatory sentence is weakened; Propositions 3 and 5 and Corollary 1 use averaged conditions and are unchanged. A uniform bound on the numbers $a_i$ of units interfering with each unit would restore the statement for all pairs, but that is an added assumption; a bound on the counts $c_i$ does not suffice (the counterexample has $C_\infty = 2$).
